newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesia coffee lower amid talk of wash-outs.
newsitem.headline: Indonesia coffee lower amid talk of wash-outs.

text.p: Indonesian coffee prices were lower on Monday in line with declines in London futures, with talk of contract wash-outs amid tight supply, traders said.
"There have been several wash-outs. But they have mostly been settled amicably between the supplier and the buyer," one trader said. "It is difficult to get beans."
The trader said the washed-out contracts were done when local export prices were at a $200-$250 per tonne discount to values in London, but the differential had since narrowed.
"The suppliers would have suffered big losses," he said. "Supply is tight while local prices are still high."

Contract wash-outs occur when the supplier is unable to physically deliver to the buyer. In such an event, the supplier will normally reimburse the buyer in cash the differential between the contracted price and the prevailing price.

The export price of grade four robusta was quoted on Monday at $1,470-$1,570 a tonne FOB (free on board) Lampung in South Sumatra, compared with $1,650-$1,700 a week ago. The local price was quoted at 3,500-3,600 rupiah/kg, against 4,000-4,100 rupiah.
London's benchmark September contract ended $5 higher at $1,600 a tonne last Friday, compared with $1,775 last week.
Traders said they expected the September contract to open unchanged to $10-$20 down when the London market opened later on Monday.
"Local prices are adjusting to the declines in London, but the FOB price discount to London is getting narrower," one trader said.

"This is because supply is very tight, and I think the market will be running out of beans over the next two months. The relatively high local price will make it more attractive to sell beans into the local market."
U.K. trade house E D & F Man said last Thursday a consensus was emerging among coffee exporters that Indonesia's current coffee crop would be at least 30 percent lower than a year ago.
It said in its June/July report the 1996/97 production, including arabicas, was estimated at 7.0 million bags, making the 1997/98 output at below 5.0 million bags.
Man attributed the shortfall to bad weather. It said a drought between May this year and April 1998 in Indonesia and linked to the El Nino weather pattern could affect output.
